subject: Archaeology
subcategory: Lost Cities of the Ancient World
title: Satellite Archaeology: Cities from Space
description: One-minute skill: Satellite Archaeology: Cities from Space.

hook.text: Sarah Parcak finds lost cities from space using satellite imagery. She has located 17 potential pyramids from her desk.

buildup.text: Infrared satellite images detect buried walls because compacted mud retains moisture differently than surrounding soil.

discovery.text: Parcak identified the lost city of Tanis in the Nile Delta and a possible Viking site in Newfoundland from satellite.

twist.text: She launched a citizen-science platform where anyone can analyze satellite images to find unknown archaeological sites.

climax.text: Satellite archaeology is now used to monitor looting in real time — tracking illegal digs in conflict zones like Syria.

punchline.text: Lost cities hide underground. Satellites see what shovels cannot.

quiz.question: How do satellites detect buried structures?
options: They use radar to bounce signals off underground walls
Infrared images detect moisture differences between compacted mud and soil
Visible-light cameras spot color changes in vegetation above ruins

details.summary: Satellite archaeology uses orbiting sensors to detect ancient cities and structures from space. Multispectral imaging reveals buried walls through vegetation stress, while radar penetrates shallow soil in deserts to map hidden features.
details.whyItMatters: Satellites survey entire countries in hours, finding sites that ground teams would take decades to discover. In unstable regions where ground access is impossible, satellites may be the only archaeological survey tool available.
takeaways: Satellites detect buried cities through vegetation and soil changes
Radar penetrates desert surfaces to reveal hidden structures
Thousands of new archaeological sites discovered since the 1990s

faq.question: How can satellites see buried structures?
faq.answer: Buried walls and roads change soil moisture and density, affecting how plants grow above them. Satellites detect these changes in near-infrared wavelengths invisible to the human eye. In deserts, radar waves penetrate dry sand to reflect off buried surfaces up to several meters deep.

faq.question: Who pioneered satellite archaeology?
faq.answer: Sarah Parcak popularized the field, using commercial satellite imagery to identify thousands of potential sites in Egypt and across the Roman world. She won the 2016 TED Prize and created the GlobalXplorer platform for citizen satellite archaeology.
